newsitem.title: UK: Clean tanker rates firm in Mideast, transatlantic.
newsitem.headline: Clean tanker rates firm in Mideast, transatlantic.

text.p: Clean tanker rates firmed in the Middle East and in the Mediterranean this week, while the U.S. continued to suck in large amounts of gasoline.

"We've seen a terrific amount of product going to the U.S. It could be coming to an end now...The shortfall seems to have been filled and I wouldn't be surprised if the market came off a little," one broker said.
Almost one million tonnes of gasoline has been chartered to cross the Atlantic since the end of December as companies seek to build stocks ahead of the summer driving season.
The transatlantic movements included an unusually large 80,000-tonne unleaded cargo at W160. Brokers E.A. Gibson said this was a "cargo size not previously seen."
Gibson said "enquiry (is) outstripping the supply of suitable tonnage in most areas" and that in some sectors "this dearth of available tonnage will continue for the balance of this month."
Middle East rates rose over the week, with several brokers citing strong Indian gasoline and gas oil demand as contributing to the firm tone.
Brokers said fixtures from the Middle East to Japan had risen to around W227.5 for 55,000 tonne vessels, from W215 at the beginning of the week.
Gibson said this size was being fixed at W280 to West Coast India off mid-February dates, "and rates are unlikely to fall due to the availability of cargoes and lack of tonnage."

Cross-Med rates surged, with 26,000 tonnes of naphtha fixed at up to W330, up from lows of about W275 a week ago. Also 70,000 tonnes from Skikda to South Korea was done at a lumpsum of $2 million, which one broker called "most impressive."
"It's a very strong (Med) market. Tonnage has been ballasting down from the Continent, which is a bit unusual," he added.
Rates in the U.K./Cont sector remained firm on good enquiry for January stems, with 25,000 tonnes of gas oil continuing to be fixed at a healthy W200, brokers said.
They said Caribbean rates were steady, with 30,000 tonnes Caribs/upcoast at W270-275 on Friday.
"Tonnage up to the end of the month has thinned out, especially for smaller ships that can get into Boston," a U.S. broker said.
